clue.text: Excellent police officer has last of grub

indicators.note: 'last of' points at the final letter of the word that follows, grub

blocks.note: super = superintendent, a senior British police rank

explanation.surface: A top-notch policeman is praised for finishing off his food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' just joins the two pieces; super is informal British shorthand for a police superintendent.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: superb and excellent both praise something as first-rate.

clue.text: Boring minutiae Gavin broadcast

indicators.note: to broadcast seed is to scatter it widely, so the letters are strewn into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone called Gavin goes on air and drones on about trivial details.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' reads as radio or television, which suits the surface of a dull presenter, but its job is to scatter the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: work lacking any imagination is dull, which is what boring means here.

clue.text: Famous rapper lost one thousand books

indicators.note: the rapper has lost something, so one letter is taken out of his name

blocks.note: EMINEM without one M (Roman numeral for a thousand)
NT = New Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: A well-known rapper has lost a thousand books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Famous' looks like it describes the rapper, but it is the definition; Eminem is the rapper and M is the Roman thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an eminent person stands out in their field and is well known for it.

clue.text: Scottish cry stifled by cheese roll

indicators.note: a cry stifled by something is smothered inside it, so the cry goes within the cheese

explanation.surface: A Scot's shout is muffled by a mouthful of cheese roll.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheese roll' reads as one snack, but 'cheese' is wordplay and 'roll' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: brioche is one kind of roll, a rich sweet French bread.

clue.text: Call into question regarding containment of soft dog

indicators.note: containment means holding something in, so the word for regarding holds the next pieces inside it

explanation.surface: Someone queries the rules about keeping a soft, cuddly dog.
explanation.walkthrough: An uncommon word, so trust the wordplay: 'regarding' is a two-letter preposition that wraps around the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though a rare formal word: oppugn comes from Latin for 'fight against' and means to dispute.

clue.text: Proprietor is worn out, about last to leave

indicators.note: 'out' as in out of joint: WORN is knocked out of its proper order
'about' means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go around the E
'last to' points at the final letter of the next word, leave

explanation.surface: A shop owner is exhausted and just about the last one to go home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worn out' looks like tiredness, and 'last to leave' like closing up, but they rearrange WORN and wrap it around E.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a proprietor is whoever holds legal title to a shop or business.

clue.text: Wallpaper glue in previous time to adhere, finally

indicators.note: 'finally' means at the end, so take the end letter of adhere

explanation.surface: Old-fashioned wallpaper glue that at last got the paper to stick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To adhere' sounds like the glue's purpose, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: flour-and-water paste is the traditional adhesive for hanging wallpaper.

clue.text: Big teenager grabs projection at seaside town

indicators.note: to grab is to take hold of, so the teenager clutches the projection inside itself

blocks.note: an arm projects from a body, or a sea arm from a coast

explanation.surface: A hulking teen snatches something at the seaside.
explanation.walkthrough: Great Yarmouth is a seaside resort on the Norfolk coast of England; a solver outside Britain may not know it, so let the wordplay do the work.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this Norfolk resort is one of many English seaside towns.

clue.text: Polite chap, a non-soldier

explanation.surface: A well-mannered man turns out not to be in the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chap' clues any man's name; here it is IAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anyone outside the armed forces is a civilian, so a non-soldier.

clue.text: Looks both ways

indicators.note: a word that works both ways reads the same forwards and backwards

blocks.note: the word for 'looks' must read the same from either end

explanation.surface: Someone checks left and right before crossing the road.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is road-safety advice, but 'both ways' says the answer is a palindrome, so only a synonym for 'looks' spelt the same backwards fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verb sense: she sees the view, she looks at the view.

clue.text: Get a new entrance

indicators.note: something made new is remade, so the letters are put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: An instruction to install a new front door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' seems to describe the entrance, but it acts on the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a gate is one kind of entrance, usually through a fence or wall.

clue.text: Courses of dried fruit, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, not a spelling, so match the word by ear

blocks.note: small dried grapes, whose name is pronounced exactly like the answer

explanation.surface: Menu courses built around dried fruit, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' suggests a meal, fitting the fruit, but it means flows of water or air.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: currents are the courses along which water, air or electricity flow.

clue.text: Object raised by poet about to move stealthily

indicators.note: a word raised is lifted and turned over, so it reads backwards
'about' as in moved about: the poet's letters are shifted around

explanation.surface: A poet lifts some item before creeping off quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' properly reverses a word in a down clue; here, in an across entry, it still turns IT round.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: going on the tips of your toes keeps footsteps quiet, so stealthy.

clue.text: Coal is exploding at informal party

indicators.note: an explosion blows things apart, so the letters land in a new order

explanation.surface: The fire goes badly wrong at a casual get-together.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a noun here, as in a church or club social, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in its noun sense: a social is a relaxed club or church gathering.

clue.text: Colour of terrier that's almost dull inside

indicators.note: 'inside' puts the shortened word within the terrier
almost the whole word, so it drops its last letter

blocks.note: Skye terrier, a Scottish dog breed
BLUR (to dull) without its last letter

explanation.surface: A question about the coat colour of a rather dull-looking dog.
explanation.walkthrough: The Skye terrier is named after the Scottish island; blur means to make dull or indistinct.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this pale, clear blue is one named colour among many.

clue.text: After gladness, I love parting word

indicators.note: 'after' orders the pieces: I and O come after the word for gladness

explanation.surface: Once the joy has faded, someone says a fond goodbye.
explanation.walkthrough: Cheerio is an informal British way of saying goodbye.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal British idiom: cheerio is said when leaving, a friendly goodbye.

clue.text: Operated my old career by chance

indicators.note: to career is to rush about wildly, so the letters go astray

explanation.surface: Someone recalls having stumbled into their old job by luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Career' reads as a job, sitting nicely with 'operated', but here it is the verb meaning to hurtle out of control.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: things that happen randomly occur by chance, without plan.

clue.text: I'd flip drink and enjoy!

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so I'D is read backwards

explanation.surface: A host says they'd throw back a drink and urges guests to have fun.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark signals an imperative: this is what a host says to invite guests to start eating.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'dig in!' urges people to start eating heartily, just as 'enjoy!' does.

clue.text: Way left for one who poses

blocks.note: a mode is a way of doing something

explanation.surface: A route left open for someone striking a pose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb (departed) but is just the letter L.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: an artist's or photographer's sitter, the person who holds a pose.

clue.text: Trees found in Chelmsford

indicators.note: what is found in a word sits inside it, so read the letters within the place name

blocks.note: letters three to six of this English town name

explanation.surface: A note that trees grow in an English town.
explanation.walkthrough: Chelmsford is the county town of Essex in England; ch-ELMS-ford holds the trees in plain sight.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the elm is one species of broadleaf tree.

clue.text: Monarch great to follow family

indicators.note: 'to follow' orders the pieces: G comes after the family word

blocks.note: g = great, as in GB for Great Britain

explanation.surface: A grand ruler takes over from his relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great' looks like praise for the monarch, but it is only the letter G.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a male sovereign is one kind of monarch.

clue.text: Awful odour's around, look sad

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so the letters of odour's are jumbled
'around' means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round LO

explanation.surface: A terrible smell hangs about, and someone looks miserable.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in 'odour's' is part of the fodder, not a possessive; 'look' is an interjection, not the verb it seems.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, somewhat literary: dolorous describes grief or sorrow.

clue.text: Part of ship keeping two nervous leaders in the doghouse

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it, so the ship part holds the letters inside
leaders go at the front, so take the first letter of nervous, here twice

blocks.note: the keel runs along a ship's bottom
two copies of the first letter of nervous

explanation.surface: Part of a ship where two jittery leaders are in disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the doghouse' is an idiom for being in disgrace, but here only 'doghouse' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the small shelter a dog sleeps in is called either name.

clue.text: Cheops ruined over time

definitions.note: the answer is plural; 'time' stands for eras in general

indicators.note: a ruined thing is wrecked, so the pharaoh's letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: The pharaoh Cheops, builder of the Great Pyramid, laid low by the passing ages.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes crumbling pyramids, which is exactly the sweep of ages the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: long, distinct stretches of history, like eras, are what time is measured in here.
